blocks.content: There is a real plant called the strangler fig. Its seed lands in the crown of a host tree, usually dropped there by a bird. It sends roots down around the trunk, wraps tighter every year, and slowly blocks the host from getting light and water.

Eventually the host tree dies and rots away inside, and the fig is left standing on its own, holding the exact shape of a tree that no longer exists. It is a genuinely strange, slightly eerie thing to see in a rainforest.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317279-232841391.png
blocks.alt: A fig seed grows roots around a host tree until the host dies and the fig stands alone

blocks.content: Software engineers borrowed this image for one of the most useful migration strategies there is: replacing a giant old monolith with new services, gradually, without ever taking the whole system down for a risky rewrite.
1. Introduction

Every large engineering org eventually inherits a monolith that has grown past the point anyone enjoys working in it. Deploys are scary, the codebase is tangled, and every team wants to move to microservices. The question is never whether to modernize it, it is how to do that without breaking the business while you do.
1.1 The Strangler Fig Plant

The strangler fig, genus Ficus, does not kill its host quickly or violently. It grows patiently, year after year, adding roots and branches around the host tree while the host keeps standing and keeps functioning, for a while.

By the time the host tree finally gives out and decays, the fig has already built its own independent structure around it. Nothing dramatic happens on the day the host dies, because the fig was never depending on that single moment to survive.

blocks.title: Where the name comes from
blocks.content: Martin Fowler popularized the term for software around 2004, explicitly naming it after this plant because the migration pattern mirrors it so closely: build alongside, take over gradually, remove the original only once it is truly empty.
1.2 From Plant To Pattern

In software, the strangler fig pattern means building new services around an existing monolith, one small piece of functionality at a time, and gradually routing traffic away from the monolith and into those new services.
The monolith keeps running the whole time. Nothing about it changes on day one. It just slowly does less and less, until one day it does nothing at all, and you can finally turn it off.
2. The Core Idea

At the center of this pattern sits a simple decision made on every single request: should this go to the old system, or the new one? Something has to make that call, and that something sits in front of both.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317280-397697980.png
blocks.alt: A routing layer sends most traffic to the old monolith and a smaller slice to a new service

blocks.content: 2.1 Growing The New Service Alongside The Old
blocks.text: 2.1 Growing The New Service Alongside The Old

blocks.content: You pick one piece of functionality, say the search feature, and you build a brand new, independent service that does just that one thing well. It gets its own codebase, its own deploy pipeline, maybe its own database.
Crucially, the monolith still has its own version of search running too. Both exist at the same time. Nobody has deleted anything yet.

["The new service is small, focused, and easy to reason about, unlike the sprawling monolith it is replacing.","It can be built with a different language, framework, or data store if that genuinely makes sense for that piece.","It ships independently, on its own schedule, without waiting on the rest of the monolith's release cycle."]
items: The new service is small, focused, and easy to reason about, unlike the sprawling monolith it is replacing.
It can be built with a different language, framework, or data store if that genuinely makes sense for that piece.
It ships independently, on its own schedule, without waiting on the rest of the monolith's release cycle.

blocks.content: 2.2 The Traffic Slice Grows Over Time
blocks.text: 2.2 The Traffic Slice Grows Over Time

blocks.content: You do not flip every user over to the new service on day one. You start small, maybe five percent of search requests, watch it hold up under real traffic, then grow that slice. Thirty percent, then seventy, then everything.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317280-801428029.png
blocks.alt: The share of traffic sent to the new service grows in stages from five percent to one hundred percent

blocks.content: Each stage is reversible. If the new service falls over at thirty percent, you dial it back to zero and the monolith absorbs the load again, because it never stopped being able to.
3. Why Not Just Rewrite From Scratch
blocks.text: 3. Why Not Just Rewrite From Scratch

blocks.content: The obvious alternative is to just stop, freeze the monolith, and spend six months building its replacement from a clean slate. Plenty of teams have tried exactly that. It rarely goes the way anyone hoped.
3.1 The Big Bang Rewrite Risk

A full rewrite means months, sometimes years, of engineering effort before a single new feature reaches a real user. Meanwhile the business still needs the old system maintained, bugs fixed, compliance changes shipped, so you are effectively paying for two systems and getting value from only one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317280-990514914.png
blocks.alt: A big bang rewrite builds silently toward one risky cutover, while a strangler migration ships small safe slices continuously

blocks.title: The graveyard of rewrites
blocks.content: Plenty of famous rewrite projects were quietly cancelled after burning a year or more of engineering time, because priorities shifted, key people left, or the new system simply never quite caught up to everything the old one already did.
3.2 Strangling Versus Rewriting

The strangler approach trades a single huge bet for a series of small, cheap ones. Every slice you cut over is a real, shippable unit of value, and every slice you have not started yet is still running safely on the monolith.

4. The Mechanics: A Routing Layer

None of this works without something sitting in front of both systems, deciding on every request whether it goes to the old monolith or the new service. That something is usually a proxy, or the API gateway you already have.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317282-775654431.png
blocks.alt: A routing layer checks a rule for each incoming request and forwards it to either the new service or the old monolith

blocks.content: 4.1 Feature Flags And Routing Rules

The routing decision is usually driven by a rule, and the simplest kind of rule is the URL path itself. Requests to slash search go to the new service, everything else still goes to the monolith. That alone gets you a long way.

For finer control, teams reach for feature flags. A flag can route by user id, by account tier, or by a random percentage bucket, which is exactly how you get that gradual five percent, thirty percent, seventy percent rollout.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317282-609682995.png
blocks.alt: A feature flag check decides per request whether traffic goes to the new service or the old monolith

blocks.content: 4.2 Implementation: A Simple Router

You do not need anything fancy to start. Here is a small routing layer that decides, per request, whether to forward to the monolith or the new service, based on a path prefix and a rollout percentage.

blocks.title: Keep the router dumb
blocks.content: The routing layer should only make forwarding decisions, never business logic. The moment it starts transforming data or making decisions about the request itself, you have built a second monolith by accident.
5. Worked Example: Migrating An E-commerce Monolith
blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Migrating An E-commerce Monolith

blocks.content: Picture a mid sized online store, one big monolith handling catalog browsing, checkout, and order history, all sharing the same codebase and the same database for years. It works, but every deploy touches all of it, and every team is scared to change anything.
5.1 Step One: Checkout Goes First

The team picks checkout to migrate first, since it is the most business critical and the most painful part of the monolith to change safely. A new checkout service is built independently, with its own database for orders in progress.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317283-420974158.png
blocks.alt: Checkout traffic goes to a new service while catalog and orders still run on the old monolith

blocks.content: The routing layer sends checkout traffic to the new service, starting small and growing over a few weeks, while catalog and order history keep running entirely on the monolith, untouched.
5.2 Step Two: Catalog Follows
Once checkout is fully cut over and stable, the team moves on to catalog. It gets its own service too, with product data replicated or migrated into a store built for fast reads.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396317283-193922970.png
blocks.alt: Catalog is migrated next and joins checkout on the new services, while orders remains on the monolith

blocks.content: Two slices are now off the monolith. Orders is the only piece still living in the original codebase, and the monolith's job has already shrunk by two thirds.
5.3 Step Three: Orders, Then The Rest
blocks.text: 5.3 Step Three: Orders, Then The Rest

blocks.content: Orders gets the same treatment: a new service, a gradual traffic shift, careful validation against the old behavior before fully cutting over. There is nothing special about it being last, it is simply the last remaining piece.
5.4 Decommissioning The Monolith

Once every feature the monolith used to serve is fully handled by a new service, and one hundred percent of traffic has been routed away for a comfortable amount of time, the monolith is finally, genuinely safe to turn off.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320443-950835068.png
blocks.alt: Once checkout, catalog, and orders all run as new services, the original monolith is decommissioned

blocks.content: The host tree does not get chopped down. By the time you remove it, it was already dead inside.
6. The Real Challenges
None of this is free. Running two systems side by side for months, sometimes years, brings its own real problems, and pretending otherwise is how migrations quietly stall.
6.1 Keeping Data In Sync

While checkout is split between old and new, an order placed through the new service still needs to show up in the monolith's order history, and vice versa, at least until every consumer of that data has also moved.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320445-182638874.png
blocks.alt: A sync job keeps the old monolith database and the new service database consistent during the transition

blocks.title: Dual writes are risky
blocks.content: Writing to both databases at once sounds simple but introduces its own failure mode: what happens when one write succeeds and the other fails. Many teams use a sync job or change data capture instead of writing to both places directly from the request path.
6.2 Routing Logic Complexity

Every new rule, every new percentage rollout, every new exception for a specific customer segment adds a bit more complexity to the routing layer. Left unmanaged, the router itself can slowly turn into a tangled mess nobody fully understands, the exact problem you were trying to escape.
Keeping routing rules simple, well tested, and reviewed like real code, not scattered configuration nobody owns, keeps this from getting out of hand.
6.3 The Half Strangled Trap

The most common way these migrations fail is not a technical failure at all. It is momentum. Checkout and catalog get migrated, everyone feels good about the progress, and then orders sits at forty percent traffic for two years because nobody prioritizes finishing it.

blocks.title: Half strangled forever
blocks.content: A monolith that is seventy percent replaced still needs to be fully maintained, monitored, and understood, because that remaining thirty percent still runs production traffic. You get none of the simplicity benefits until the very last piece is actually gone.
7. Real World Usage

This is not a theoretical pattern. It is one of the most common ways real companies actually get off an aging monolith, precisely because it lets the business keep shipping while engineering modernizes underneath it.

["Large e-commerce and fintech platforms use it to peel critical flows like payments and checkout off a legacy core, one flow at a time.","Companies migrating between cloud providers or data centers often strangle traffic over gradually rather than cutting over all at once.","It shows up constantly in \"monolith to microservices\" migration writeups from engineering teams at established companies, precisely because the big bang alternative kept failing them."]
items: Large e-commerce and fintech platforms use it to peel critical flows like payments and checkout off a legacy core, one flow at a time.
Companies migrating between cloud providers or data centers often strangle traffic over gradually rather than cutting over all at once.
It shows up constantly in "monolith to microservices" migration writeups from engineering teams at established companies, precisely because the big bang alternative kept failing them.

blocks.content: 8. The Interview Angle

If an interviewer asks how you would safely migrate a large legacy system to a new architecture, reaching for a full rewrite is usually the wrong answer, and reaching for the strangler fig pattern is usually a strong one.
8.1 How To Frame The Answer

Name the pattern, explain the routing layer that decides old versus new per request, and walk through picking one low risk slice first, growing traffic to it gradually, and only decommissioning the old system once nothing depends on it anymore.

blocks.title: A strong interview answer
blocks.text: I would not rewrite the whole system at once, that is a high risk bet with no incremental payoff. Instead I would put a routing layer in front of the monolith, pick one well isolated piece of functionality to rebuild as a new service, and shift traffic to it gradually using a feature flag, watching error rates the whole way. Once that slice is fully migrated and stable, I would repeat it for the next piece, and only remove the monolith once every piece of functionality has a home elsewhere.

blocks.content: 8.2 The Full Migration Timeline
Zooming out, the whole migration looks like a steady march: start fully on the monolith, strangle one slice at a time, and end with the monolith gone entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320446-115066618.png
blocks.alt: The full migration timeline moves from all monolith through each strangled slice to the monolith being decommissioned

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["The pattern is named after a real plant that grows around a host tree and slowly replaces it, exactly the shape of this migration.","A routing layer decides per request whether traffic goes to the old monolith or a new service, usually driven by path rules or feature flags.","Traffic to the new service grows gradually, in reversible stages, instead of one risky cutover.","It beats a big bang rewrite because every slice ships real value and every failure is contained to one small piece.","The two hardest parts are keeping data in sync across both systems, and actually finishing instead of stalling half migrated.","It is a genuinely common real world strategy, and a strong, concrete answer to \"how would you migrate this legacy system safely\" in an interview."]
items: The pattern is named after a real plant that grows around a host tree and slowly replaces it, exactly the shape of this migration.
A routing layer decides per request whether traffic goes to the old monolith or a new service, usually driven by path rules or feature flags.
Traffic to the new service grows gradually, in reversible stages, instead of one risky cutover.
It beats a big bang rewrite because every slice ships real value and every failure is contained to one small piece.
The two hardest parts are keeping data in sync across both systems, and actually finishing instead of stalling half migrated.
It is a genuinely common real world strategy, and a strong, concrete answer to "how would you migrate this legacy system safely" in an interview.
